guidedMeditation.speaker: Kadam Kyle
guidedMeditation.text:
We can feel that our spiritual guide, in the aspect of Je Tsongkhapa, mixes with our root mind — not our heart — like water mixing with water. We can feel that everything dissolves into this inseparable bliss and emptiness of our guru's mind. There is not even a meditator left.

Everything is inseparable bliss and emptiness. We can notice that in this space, there is no higher or lower, here or there, hot or cold, self or other. Everything is very peaceful and comfortable, joyful and harmonious, wonderful. Everything is equal in the peace of emptiness.

Then in our own time, we can gradually arise from our practice.

postMeditation.speaker: Kadam Kyle
postMeditation.text:
I didn't mean for us to do that meditation in that session, but there was a mystery Heart Jewel prayers, which I don't think we do in this class. But anyway, we did Heart Jewel. We dissolved the guru into the heart, and that was that. So then we did that meditation.

I just took it as a sign that we should do that meditation for many reasons. One is I think we're sort of — it's our first class in our term-ish — and so it's nice to think that meditation has everything in it. It has so much depth and profundity. It's a practice for reliance on the spiritual guide. It has enlightenment in it. It has everything in between. That's the whole path, from reliance on the spiritual guide to attaining full enlightenment. Everything else in between is just the journey there. And those are all in one practice, one meditation. So it felt right to do that meditation.

And then also because we have our special all-day retreat coming up at the end of the month on learning how to meditate on our root mind, our very subtle mind — at first kind of like according to sutra, and then according to tantra. Since we have that coming up in a couple of weeks, called Infinite Mind, it felt nice to just do that meditation, or something very similar to that meditation.

postMeditation.speaker: Kadam Kyle
postMeditation.text:
Next week we'll have our new and spiffy TTP contracts. The preferred ink is blood that you sign with. But if you don't want to do that, then there are other options too. Black or blue is welcome too. No, just kidding.

Good job. There was a big sleeping party in the meditation, I noticed. I couldn't tell how many people were sleeping, but I think we were at half the room. We might have been at three-quarters of the room. I'm not being critical by any means. I'm just sort of noting for myself and thinking, what can we do to not all be asleep during the practice? Over time, it is good to know kind of why we personally fall asleep in meditation and what precedes that, and then how to take some actions to prevent that.

shantidevaReading.text:
[12] Through giving all, I shall attain the nirvana of a Buddha
And my bodhichitta wishes will be fulfilled.
I give up everything for the sake of living beings,
Who are the supreme objects of giving.

[13–14] Since I have given up this body
For the happiness of living beings,
It will always be theirs to beat, to revile
Or even to kill if they please.

Even if they play with it,
Mock it or humiliate it,
Since I have given this body to others,
What is the point of holding it dear?

[15–16] Therefore, in whatever I do,
I will never cause harm to others;
And whenever anyone encounters me,
May it never be meaningless for them.

Whether those who encounter me
Generate faith or anger,
May it always be the cause
Of their fulfilling all their wishes.

[17] May all those who harm me —
Whether verbally or by other means —
And those who otherwise insult me
Thereby create the cause to attain enlightenment.

[18] May I become a protector for the protectorless,
A guide for those who travel on the road,
And, for those who wish to cross the water,
May I become a boat, a ship or a bridge.

[19] May I become an island for those seeking dry land,
A lamp for those needing light,
A place of rest for those who desire one,
And a servant for those needing service.

[20] To benefit all living beings,
May I become a treasury of wealth,
Powerful mantras, potent medicine,
A wish-fulfilling tree and a wish-granting cow.

[21–22] Just like the great elements such as earth,
And like eternal space,
May I become the basis from which everything arises
For sustaining the life of countless living beings;

And, until they have passed beyond sorrow,
May I sustain all forms of life
Throughout the realms of living beings
That reach to the ends of space.

dataShares.speaker: Ryan
dataShares.text:
I said to Kyle earlier this morning that I noticed that certain people trigger me. And it's probably a creation by my mind — maybe the way they talk or they don't talk, some bias. But this afternoon, I noticed that also certain questions trigger me. So this afternoon, someone asked me, 'So Ryan, are you coming to the self-generation or completion class?' And I lost it again. And I decided to give that person a piece of my mind. And I said, 'Did you come to the Lamrim class yesterday? Are you coming next Saturday to the workshop How to Restart Your Life?'

But I lost it. And I thought to myself, why am I losing it at certain topics too? It's a question I have to investigate, because I'm going to teach it.

Regarding this meditation, I got to be honest — I started the meditation, I have no clue what I'm supposed to do with this dissolving. First, I got irritated. What am I doing for 20 minutes now? But then I thought to myself, okay, screw the whole thing. Let me go back to my breath. Let me just enjoy the company of this sangha. I'm sitting with beautiful people here. Teachers, people who cook dinners for everyone, people who work education, people who scrub toilets. So that's what I did. I just enjoyed the company. So my mind wasn't dissolving with some gurus, but my heart was dissolving with this sangha, with each of you. So I was good.

dataShares.speaker: Kadam Kyle
dataShares.text:
Yeah, thanks Ryan. Regarding the first point, it is helpful just to start to notice that. Like why are we getting annoyed in certain situations, but not in others? And it's just clearly coming from our mind. That's why we're getting annoyed. But we have to become aware of what that reason is. And start to undo it and unravel it. Generally speaking, it's always because we're attached to something. Every time we're annoyed or angry, we're attached to something. There's never a moment of anger that is not linked to a type of attachment.

And so we can always ask, if we're trying to figure out where's the anger coming from, we can ask, okay, what am I attached to? And then that will give us a pretty clear answer.

Regarding the meditation, mixing the mind with the guru's mind — maybe at first it can feel a little bit abstract or general. Over time we can learn some tips and tricks on how to improve that. But what you did makes sense. There's never a point to resent a meditation. At some point if you realize, I've got nothing, I'm totally lost — there's no point to then sit in resentment or anger. It's like, okay, well, I've got to do something that's going to bring me forward in my practice. Maybe it's just being accepting and practicing patient acceptance, not knowing. That's a great meditation to do in that moment.

Meditation means gom. Familiarize. That's the Tibetan word. It just means to familiarize our mind with virtue. What's the point of a puja? It's an hour and 45 minutes of familiarizing our mind with virtue. But if we're not familiarizing our mind with virtue because we got lost or confused or whatever, then we just find our way in to do that in the practice.

dataShares.speaker: Mimi
dataShares.text: My data share is related to the empowerment at the festival. I have been thinking a lot about what Kadam Morton said in the very beginning about us being a fortunate assembly. And how we — or Buddha Shakyamuni — created the karma to be amongst this assembly. And how I felt at the festival that we were the fortunate assembly creating this karma to be connected with Buddha Shakyamuni. And how that's all connected to what we're learning in our book about turning the wheel of Dharma, beseeching the Buddhas not to pass away. And how that all really came alive in my heart. Just so happy about that.

dataShares.speaker: Kadam Kyle
dataShares.text:
Thanks, Mimi. It's lovely. It's just connecting to the karmic creation of the experience that we're in. Everything is just like a karmic appearance that will cease instantly if the karma for it to appear ceases. Just instantly cease. No warning.

So if there's no karma for us to appear — what we're appearing, our fortunate spiritual life — then it will just disappear. Just like a dream disappearing. And so it's so helpful to try to connect to: there's this set of really special karma we've made in our mental continuum. It's all coming together for these beautiful and spiritual experiences and appearances. But it's also tenuous from a point of view. It's just linked to those causes. Like things seen in a dream.

And so it kind of behooves us to keep creating those causes as much as possible. And dedicating for them and wishing for them. But being grateful for them while they're there.

dataShares.speaker: Anne
dataShares.text:
This isn't related to TTP but it has been my main practice the last two weeks. I keep finding these very basic practices that I've never actually done. Like reducing self-cherishing. I've been hearing about it for a while and I never really tried it. And just this notion that whatever little bugaboo I have during the day — that I really am just one of eight billion people. And how relaxing that is to remember.

And then really making the connection for the first time that my problem is only as big — it's directly related to how important I see myself. The more important I consider myself the bigger my problem is and the more difficult it is to solve. And if I don't consider myself that important, if I just consider myself one of eight billion people, my problem is not a big deal and it is very easy to solve. In fact it's probably not even a problem at all.

And then so all week long whenever I had a problem I just remembered, well yeah, you're one of eight billion people. Not a big deal in the big scheme of things. And then turning my mind directly to three people I knew who actually had a big problem. And it saved me so much stupid mental energy. It really smoothed things out for me.

dataShares.speaker: Kadam Kyle
dataShares.text:
That's lovely. So really trying to move based on that reason: I am only one, others are countless, their problems are far greater than the suffering I experience now. Which is one of the reasons we use in equalizing self with others — to develop love for others and to get out of the self-cherishing mind.

So you're really practically doing it by having an exact plan. The second that self-centered mind came up, moving your mind to three people. Using it as a ricochet. When I'm doing this — boom — moving your mind immediately to those three people. Instead of just perseverating, kind of obsessing. Digging a big hole of misery.

I appreciate how specific and exact the practice is. Because it's very measurable then. If I'm doing it or not. Instead of, 'I'm generally going to love people when I'm in pain.' What in the world does that mean? How are you going to know whether you're doing that or not? What's the metric? When we make it really concrete like this, you just know whether you're doing it or not. And that's fantastic. And then we change.

dataShares.speaker: Marianne
dataShares.text:
I wanted to share something because I was talking to Dale about it earlier and it did kind of seem clear to me regarding karma. It was about that thing that happened at the festival. After five days of being in bed, I wanted to go to the last session. And there was a communication problem and then I didn't get to go and I got super deluded and super mad. I just wanted to go to that last session so bad.

Fortunately, Suzanne was there to witness that and she was just so strong and she was like, they didn't do that on purpose. They weren't trying to mess you up. It's just these things happen. You just didn't get to go. And I was like, I am so attached to something that I wanted.

And then I was thinking about it a little bit more and I was like, oh my God, this is the karma I've been purifying since the beginning of the year. I've come to this festival and now I have the same karma ripening — horrible anger in the middle of the festival — which is the karma I have of being left and left out.

In a way, yeah, I didn't go to the last session, but that karma has not been purified yet. And maybe this is hopefully part of the purification. And it was so clear and it was so much better to be like, oh, this is the path. I am purifying this karma with a really stupid reaction to something. You've got to deal with it. And you can purify it. It's not gone yet, but it might be on its way to being gone.

dataShares.speaker: Kadam Kyle
dataShares.text:
Two things there. One is just the value of sangha. So ten points for Suzanne. That's what a good sangha friend does, right? They don't let us increase our delusions. That's not what a sangha friend's for. Sometimes we want someone to massage our delusions. But that's not really what a sangha friend's for. They're for our liberation. And as long as we trust each other and love each other, then it's amazing when a sangha friend can say, come on, let's not do this, let's go in this direction instead.

And then the second point — you're right. It's just a karmic appearance. You can be at Manjushri Center, or nearby, flown all the way across the ocean, have all the conditions put together, and still not be able to get in the building. And it's not because of anyone else. It's just our karma. And as you said, it's like a karma of abandoning people. If that's our experience, that's obviously showing us some kind of karma in our mind.

And it sounds like you were able to kind of get there in the end, which is fantastic. It's very brave and courageous to get to that conclusion. It takes a lot of humility to do that in our life. Like, okay, this is my lot. This is my practice. This is part of my path. Me and my guru and my sangha — and we're going to definitely uproot this karma in the mind.

dataShares.speaker: Kristin
dataShares.text:
I think the main takeaways for me from NEDC are just an incredible sense of gratitude to everyone who helped put it together. Kadam Dana mentioned it being like a family reunion. And it really felt that way. You could tell that people were hosting and so many people gave up their rooms and were in tents so that other people could sleep in their rooms during the festival. Everybody was pitching in.

And this idea of having fun when practicing Dharma, and basically if you're not having fun, you're not practicing Dharma — I think was a really great theme. I have noticed a lot and already even today forgotten to apply as I was cleaning the house and being agitated.

Lastly, I really appreciated the deeper insight into the Liberating Prayer and in particular this idea of the importance of engaging in a relationship with the Bodhisattva community at the beginning, and the importance of requesting blessings. Kadam Morton sort of suggested that we contemplate this idea that happiness is directly from blessings and indirectly from our virtuous activities. And I sort of was mulling that over and I'm thinking it's because a blessing is transforming our mind from a negative to a positive state. So it's that idea of really intentionally setting up for that transformation and asking for that.

dataShares.speaker: Kadam Kyle
dataShares.text:
Thanks Kristin. It's a really nice point about the kindness of others and that events like that are basically created by the kindness of other sangha friends who are just trying to make us happy.

And a good reminder too about that word 'fun.' Having fun practicing Dharma. It's a nice example again of using synonyms, which we talked about a few times. Having fun practicing Dharma, or practicing Dharma like a child at play. Or practicing joyful effort. Or a mind that delights in virtue. These are all synonyms. We're trying to talk about the same thing. It's just sometimes a word triggers our mind in a different way, in a helpful way.

dataShares.speaker: Fran
dataShares.text:
Listening to people talk about NEDC, I'm just reminded that the theme of it was faith and I'm always very grateful for my faith. That even when I'm struggling with my practice, or I don't want to do this, or this seems like it's too hard — I cling to the fact that I do believe.

There are a couple of things that were mentioned. In the Liberating Prayer — 'through your compassionate intention, your blessings and virtuous deeds, and my strong wish to rely on you' — that Buddha Shakyamuni has done all the work. It's his compassionate intention, his blessings, his virtuous deeds, and I just have to rely on that and follow the instructions.

And the second thing — I don't remember whether it was Morton or Gen Sangthin who said Geshe-la has walked the path and we just have to put our feet in his footsteps and just follow along. The hard work has already been done for us. So I'm just grateful for my faith and the reminder of that.

dataShares.speaker: David
dataShares.text:
I've been thinking about dependent relationship over the last couple weeks and there were two different circumstances that really illustrated this very clearly — the different roles that I play. Over Labor Day weekend I was in Ohio for a friend's wedding. Happened to be right next to where my in-laws live, so we were staying with my in-laws. Then we'd drive 20 minutes and spend four or five hours with a bunch of friends who all knew each other and then go back and sleep with the parents. It was this crazy whiplash and I'm like, who am I? What's going on right now?

Then the same thing happened this week on Friday. It was like, went to meditation in the park and then a few people came over afterwards and then some of them left and then a bunch of colleagues who were visiting from overseas came over and I was like — sangha friend and then this colleague person — and there was a period where their groups were mixing and I was like, I'm trying to hold on to something here and it's very uncomfortable to try to hold on to these two roles simultaneously. At one point I realized I was doing it and I just kind of let go, and then my wife came home and then all of a sudden I'm a husband person.

It reminded me of a teaching that you can't be the thing because you're made up of all these different parts. You take out none of the individual roles as the real me, but without any of them, there's nothing left. I just sort of saw that very clearly but I'd like to remember it more — use that to realize there's nothing really here.

dataShares.speaker: Kadam Kyle
dataShares.text:
Yeah, thanks David. It's a good way to do the emptiness meditation. Sometimes it's easier than the parts on the body and mind. We just do kind of the role-based parts. We just think: I'm not a husband inherently because sometimes I'm a co-worker. But I'm not a co-worker because when I'm a co-worker I'm not the husband. You just take that out. Okay, so I'm not a co-worker, I'm not a husband, and you just go through all the different roles, and then there's just nothing to be a self. Because we're not any of those roles.

And then when we get stuck switching a little bit, it's because we're grasping at one role. Thinking it's somehow really us. And when we start to see it's all just play — it's just all emptiness appearing as this or that — then it's just very easy and flexible and nice.

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text:
I sent out a request to everyone via WhatsApp for us to identify one of the 26 delusions — the six root delusions and the 20 secondary delusions — and to choose one to work on for a period of time. We're going to switch them at some point because basically what's going to happen where we're at in the book is we're finishing up with dedication and then into giving and then taking the Bodhisattva vows and then a couple of little bits and pieces. And then we go into conscientiousness and then guarding alertness.

Conscientious is pretty much a part of the mind that is vigilant against delusions and increasing virtues. It's kind of like the CEO of the whole Dharma practice — because it's the one that's trying to marshal all the mental factors to block against delusion and to increase virtue.

So all this dedication — when we dedicate, what we always want to do is imagine the result of the dedication. And so with our one delusion that we're trying to focus on and zoom in on and oppose, what I want to encourage us to do over this week ahead is: one, to constantly dedicate every virtuous action towards the elimination of that delusion. Just funnel all the merit into that. Like an assault on one change. You can then throw in, 'and for the benefit of all living beings.' Or, 'I'm going to conquer this one delusion for the benefit of all living beings.' So it's kind of a perfection. But it's all directed at one.

And then when we dedicate, what we're going to do is imagine what does it really look like to have a cessation of that delusion. And this is a very, very interesting practice. What we'll find as we go through the different delusions is the generic image of the cessation of a delusion will be very unclear with a lot of them.

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text:
[Class discussion on what the cessation of miserliness would look like. Alexis suggests 'freedom.' Mimi suggests 'giving.' Fran adds 'spontaneously giving without the thinking of I should give.' KK asks what the motive would be — Fran says 'to help somebody.' KK draws out that it requires a huge amount of love. Sumit adds it involves having a realization of the emptiness of the I. Anne says you'd have to realize nothing belongs to you. Ryan describes seeing a practitioner at the Northeast celebration who seems free of miserliness to his time.]

So now we're getting more into not just the mental state, but the tools to help us get there. Because maybe we're not going to imagine a mind when we're trying to imagine no miserliness. We might not be able to perfectly imagine a mind that has uprooted all self-grasping, has a perfect realization of love, has gained precise understandings of the working of karma. Maybe all of those experiences all at once is just a little bit much.

But what we want to do is, as we start to imagine these realizations, get closer. Move from just a little bit of peace to a little bit more of what it really looks like for us. One of the ways to do it is to see other examples and rejoice in them. A second way is to picture what it would look like in our own life. Even a little bit visually, or mentally, have an image of what it would look like to oppose that miserliness. For example, we're tired at the end of our work day, and someone asks us for our time. What does it look like to have completely overcome any trace of miserliness in that moment?

As Geshe-la says in Ocean of Nectar, the hair stands up on the back of our neck, because we're like, I'm going to get to give! The benefits of giving are so incredible, and I know I'm creating a pure land from this one action of giving.

So whenever we practice dedication, or every time we do something virtuous over this week ahead, let's start practicing this. One: we just think, okay, doing the dishes, or being nice to this person, or meditating — this positive action — may I benefit all living beings, and especially through overcoming this specific delusion. And then when we dedicate, we imagine what does that really look like. The me-version of having conquered this delusion. We're not aiming for perfection. We're just aiming on something that's better than yesterday's model.

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text:
So, page 123. General dedication. 'To the merit collected from prostration, offering, confession, and other virtues, may the suffering of all sentient beings be dispelled.' That's our always-dedication.

Dedication for the sick. 'May I become the doctor, medicine, and nurse for all sentient beings throughout the universe for as long as they remain in sickness.' We should pray to be able to answer the various needs of all those suffering from disease. Through the power of such prayers and their heightened concentration, it is possible for advanced Bodhisattvas to manifest actual medicine to be taken by those who are ill. Even though these powers are beyond us now, we should dedicate our merit to be able to benefit others as much as possible in the future.

To make our prayers deep and effective, we should first think of the pains and misery that the sick experience. We can meditate on those who are confined to a hospital, those sick and dying alone, without a friend to care for them. And those whose tears we have seen, and whose cries we have heard. Then we generate compassion toward these suffering beings, and pray to become a doctor, medicine, and nurse for all those who are sick.

This dedication is a very wonderful meditation. Step one: you empathize with people's pain, and you try to bring it alive — those who are sick. Step two: you develop compassion on the basis of that empathy, that exchanging self with others. What is it really like from their point of view to be forgotten about in a home somewhere, where you are getting treatment and no one comes to visit you, and the whole family doesn't want to bother anymore? What is it really like from that person's point of view? That is step two. On the basis of that empathy, that exchanging self with others, we develop compassion, we think about the pain that is there.

Then step three: we make a wish to protect that person. And four: in our dedication, we dedicate to actually become the answer to their prayers, and what they are looking for. We can even imagine being that. I wish I could appear as countless beings to be kind and loving doctors, and nurses, and support staff, and friends, and medicine for the people there. You can imagine sending that out, for example, to just the hospitals in New York City — of which there are tons of hospitals. There are tons of people in very complicated health situations just here. What would it be like to really be a healer for them, an answer to their prayers.

As Bodhisattvas, or training Bodhisattvas, we just have a special place in our heart for the people suffering from sickness.

mainTeaching.speaker: Dale
mainTeaching.text: In the section on suffering that you just went over, and how you should open your heart to that — what happens if when you walk in to a hospital or a nursing home, your PTSD is triggered, and you just want to run? That's what happened recently to me, because of my husband. I had to go to the hospital to pick up a friend who was being released, and I was holding my breath. The thought of having to be there triggers that anxiety in me. So I don't quite know how to deal with that.

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text:
With this kind of thing, there's sort of two sides. One is to explore what does the healing look like. With grief of a lost husband, someone that you love dearly — what does a complete cessation of that grief look like? Kind of like with our imagination practice that we did with the delusions. It's nice to just start imagining what would it look like to reach that place of total healing here. It's not saying we have to be there today, but it's really nice to start imagining that. If we don't start imagining and envisioning what that's like, it's going to feel pretty tough to move towards.

On the other side, it's a reminder to take our pain into becoming a healer for others. When someone's a real healer, usually they heal the pain that they dealt with, and that pain gets transmuted into healing. And so the pain becomes a strength. It's like a Lojong practice, transforming adversity. I'm using my pain of grief, or of sickness, or of disappointment as the basis of my being able to heal others.

Then going into a hospital setting like that will have a very different feeling. You'll feel like a healer moving through this environment of people who are just like you, who need the help that you needed. And then a very confident feeling will come — I'm actually a healer moving through this space. And I have medicine blood at my heart, and I can help people who've dealt with what I've dealt with. Then it flips on its head, and our pain becomes our strength.

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text:
Dedication to relieve hunger and thirst. 'May a rain of food and drink dispel the sufferings of hunger and thirst. During the aeon of severe famine, may I myself become food and drink for all.' By dedicating our merit in this way, we create the cause to become a benefactor of all living beings in the future. At the present time, the hunger and thirst experienced in this world are small compared to that which will be experienced during a future age.

We're making our dedications beyond just this world and this realm. The Buddhas are like these cosmic beings that are playing a game of chess over a millions-of-lifetime arc. They're thinking about countless worlds, countless aeons. And so we want to start emulating that big vision. Dedicating and wishing for goodness and happiness in those future times. Not just here and now.

These kind of dedications are incredibly pure, too, because they're so not useful for the self-cherishing mind right now. We're not going to see the results. So they have a kind of beauty to them, an elegance to them.

Dedication to fulfill the wishes of sentient beings. A mother full of love and compassion for children prays continually for their welfare, success, and prosperity. With great love and compassion for all sentient beings, we should pray to become whatever it might be that others require. 'May I become an inexhaustible treasury for those who are poor and destitute. In accordance with sentient beings' needs, may I become whatever they desire, and always be at their disposal.' This concludes the first four of the five preparatory practices for accumulating merit. What remains is to train our minds in the expansive practice of selfless giving.

dedication.speaker: Kadam Kyle
dedication.text: Let's take a little breather here. Let's come back at 6:19 approximately. We'll just do a little dedication now. We can think of the virtues we've collected through practicing, meditating, discussing. May all living beings find lasting peace of mind, enlightenment. We can make any other personal prayers and dedications, for example, to overcome our delusion of choice.

chantedPrayers.text: Liberating Prayer O Blessed One, Shakyamuni Buddha, precious Treasury of Compassion, Bestower of Supreme Inner Peace. You who love all beings without exception are the source of happiness and goodness, and you guide us to the liberating path. Your body is a wish-fulfilling jewel, your speech is supreme, purifying nectar, and your mind is refuge for all living beings. With folded palms I turn to you, Supreme unchanging Friend. I request from the depths of my heart, please give me the light of your wisdom to dispel the darkness of my mind and to heal my mental continuum. Please nourish me with your goodness, that I in turn may nourish all beings with an unceasing banquet of delight. Through your compassionate intention, your blessings and virtuous deeds, and my strong wish to rely upon you, may all suffering quickly cease and all happiness and joy be fulfilled, and may holy Dharma flourish forevermore.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
Just take a couple of minutes to imagine what it would be like to be completely free of our delusion of choice. Not just an absence of our delusion, but a mind that is actively opposing it, through its opposite. We can all just see if we can imagine what some similitude would be like of this experience. And then we can gradually arise from our practice.

[Sumit asks about how to know if dedication is working. KK responds:] Anything that has a long-term karmic effect — it's just hard to get a proper signal about whether we're going in the right direction or not. Because there's a lag. There will be changes. Geshe-la even talks about this with taking and giving — we'll notice because we'll have reduced self-grasping, and we might even have dreams that we're purifying in certain ways.

Sometimes it's very stark, like I've shared the example in this class before about when I was dedicating to stop drinking. It was like a month, and then one month later, from doing that every day with every virtuous action, I woke up, and I had no interest to drink anymore. It was vanished. I wanted to, wanted to, wanted to, wanted to, wanted to. No lessening, actually. Wanted to, wanted to, went to bed, woke up. No interest. Poof.

If we notice something isn't changing at all, it's usually not a sign that our dedication is the problem. It's a sign that we're creating more of the karma that we're trying to dedicate to undo. Or we're not really dealing with the delusions that lead to that experience.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
[Alexis shares about choosing faith as her delusion to overcome. She got into a beautiful experience of imagining strong faith, but then intrusive, discouraged thoughts came in — 'What if this doesn't happen? You're lying to yourself. What if nothing changes?' She asks how to work through that discomfort.]

With these kind of thoughts, the approach is actually a very strict one. It's a practice akin to the clarity of mind meditation. What we need to get into the hang of is basically: this is just a thought. And I don't need to think every thought. I don't need to listen to every thought. And I definitely don't need to wrestle with these thoughts because they're totally absurd.

They're not you. They're not actually coming from you. They're coming from some weird, creepy-crawly delusions that are lurking in the mind, which are not us. We're doing this incredibly beautiful virtuous thing. We're even getting some experience. They get threatened, and they start spewing their vitriol at us.

We have to get in the hang of treating them like an evil minister or counselor, like in our little boardroom of our mind. Every time they talk, I don't listen to them at all. There's nothing they say that's true. I'm not trying to actually placate them. I'm not trying to disprove them even, because that's taking them seriously, and they don't deserve to be taken seriously.

So we're treating them like static, like noise. The phrase that's really nice is: 'This is just a thought.' That's like the mantra, and we use it like a sort of sword that we stab through those Mara thoughts. Because they're not based on any truth at all. They're only there to ruin our fun.

Those thoughts aren't based in an evaluation of actually how we are. They're just discouraged, self-attacking thoughts. If you improve, they'll always keep attacking. They're actually not evaluating how we're actually doing. They're just there to attack us and bring us down. So to placate them and play their game — be like, 'I'm actually really great, thank you very much' — is saying what you're saying is kind of right, and I'm going to defeat you in an argument. But they're not right.

There are another type of discouraged thought where we make a clear error, and then we get down on ourselves for the clear error. That's a different case. In those cases, sometimes we do have to bring ourselves up. This is different. This is just attacking us for no reason.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
So we are on training the mind in giving. Just as a heads up, a bunch of weeks ago, I read this story about Sadaprarudita. I'm not going to reread it word for word, because I have done that, but when we skip that in a moment, please don't think it's being skipped. It's because you already got the transmission of that story. It's a beautiful story about guru devotion and giving.

Training the mind in giving. Shantideva declares: 'From this moment on, without any sense of loss, I shall give away my body, and likewise my wealth, and my virtues amassed throughout the three times — past, present, and future — to help all living beings, my mothers.' This is one of the citations that the Lojong teachers used when they taught taking and giving, along with some from Nagarjuna and others.

It is beyond our ability at present to make such a bold declaration as this, but by training our mind in a proper way, we will certainly be able to engage in such selfless giving in the future. We can destroy our attachment to our body and our possessions by meditating on their shortcomings and lack of essence — their emptiness — and if we think deeply about the many benefits that arise from giving what we have to others, we will eventually be able to emulate the deeds of the Bodhisattvas.

It is important to train our mind well now in the thought of giving up our body and possessions, because as Shantideva next points out, we'll have to give up everything we own at the time of death anyway. If, as we pass from this life, we cling possessively to our body and wealth, we will experience great inner torment and plant the seeds of a lower rebirth. Therefore, before the time comes when everything will be taken from us involuntarily, it is wise to acquaint ourselves with the thought of giving what we own to others. To be able to give our body and possessions to others voluntarily is the best way to extract meaning from them.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
Certain higher beings who have trained their mind to overcome attachment and self-cherishing, and in addition have meditated upon great compassion and the profound view of emptiness, are able, if the need arises, to surrender their body without difficulty and give it to others. They experience no sense of loss from this practice and are able to view their body as if it were an insignificant object. Whether we can practice in the same way, however, is doubtful. As long as we are governed by self-cherishing, it would be more harmful than helpful to sacrifice something as precious as our body. Furthermore, it is a mistake to give up this precious human vehicle unless there is a great need and purpose for doing so. Yet it is still an important practice to rejoice in the actions of those Bodhisattvas who can actually give away their body and possessions, and to pray that someday we will be able to do the same.

So you think about a Bodhisattva, and they've gained a realization of exchanging self with others. At that point, they think 'I' on respect to all living beings. In their psychological experience, every being is as validly labeled as self or me as this collection of aggregates is. Self, self, self, self — me, me, me, me — all living beings of the six realms. They have this mind that's at one with the whole of life. And they're just thinking, I want to benefit the whole of the body of life.

So for that person, if the time came where they realized sacrificing one little body is the way to help the entire whole in the greatest way possible, they're like, yeah, sure. No problem. The Bodhisattva, when we realize emptiness — we just think the body is just an appearance, it's like a clod of earth. It's not us. We don't identify the self with the body at all. It's like a pile of stones.

Having given up my body completely, it does not matter to me what sentient beings choose to do with it. For their pleasure, I have given up my body to others. Let them play with it, ridicule, beat, or even kill it, if it so pleases them. Because I have given it to others, what is the point of holding my body dear any longer?

If such a high-minded being were to sit between two people, one who cut them with a knife, while the other anointed their body with perfume, the Bodhisattva would look upon them both with equal love and compassion. Because they think of their body as like a tree. If you just see a tree and someone's cutting it down, you're like — I like the tree, but, yes, okay, chop away. And if they're anointing the tree — oh, that's cool, you're putting some perfume on a tree. It's just like an inanimate object.

No matter if others harm me physically or insult me verbally, may whatever they do become the cause of their enlightenment. May I become a protector for the protectorless. May I become a guide for those who travel, and a boat, a ship, and a bridge for those who wish to cross the water. May I become an island for those in trouble, a lamp for those who travel in darkness. May I become an abode and a place of rest for those desiring one, and a servant for those who want a servant. May I become a wish-fulfilling jewel for those with special wishes, a treasure of wealth, powerful mantras, and effective medicine. In all my lives, may I become a wish-fulfilling tree, and an inexhaustible wish-granting cow that satisfies all beings.

Just as the great elements of earth, water, and so forth support the life of sentient beings, so may I too become the foundation of sustenance for all. May I become whatever is beneficial for all sentient beings in their realms, reaching to the ends of space, until they attain complete and unsurpassable enlightenment.

Why is it necessary to make prayers like this? If we wish to develop the precious bodhichitta, we must cultivate a beneficial intention towards all sentient beings. We can train ourselves in this way by paying close attention to the situation of others. Whenever we see sentient beings suffering, we should think, what can I do to dispel their misery and bring them happiness? We should train our mind constantly with this beneficial thought.

So these are just some additional dedication prayers where we're imagining being an answer to everyone's prayers, everywhere. And over time, just take time with these verses and think about them. What's it like to be a boat, a ship, and a bridge for those in the world? May I be a bridge between two parties who are fighting. What's it like to be an island for those in trouble? It's like being a refuge for people in fear. A lamp for those who travel in darkness — giving wisdom and guiding people and giving people a way forward. We can mine these verses and see the metaphors as our teachings and practical advice.

practiceDiscussion.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceDiscussion.text: Okay, everyone, thank you. Come one, come all. Anyone have anything that you think we should practice in the break ahead?

practiceDiscussion.speaker: Fran
practiceDiscussion.text: I have a tendency to not recognize things as something to be dedicated, as something virtuous to be dedicated, so I would like to make an effort to recognize opportunities to dedicate.

practiceDiscussion.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceDiscussion.text: Yeah. And then can we specifically be dedicating?

practiceDiscussion.speaker: Fran
practiceDiscussion.text: Dedicating for my delusion, to end my delusion, and for the benefit of all living beings.

practiceDiscussion.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceDiscussion.text:
For all those folk. Yeah, that's nice. It's kind of like, you know, the Geshe Ben Gungyel practice of watching the mind — the dark stones and the light stones. With watching the mind in general, that can be a little tricky because there's so many thoughts all day. But it's nice sometimes to choose one specific practice and use that as the axis of counting the stones.

After every action, every positive action, if we remember to dedicate, we tally up a positive stone. And then if we forget, we won't notice right then, obviously, because we forgot, but then later we can tally up a dark stone. And this is a great way to do the practice because it kind of simplifies it and compresses it into something a bit more manageable.

A fun way to do this too, is to make a prediction of how it's going to go beforehand. How many positive ones — like what ratio? Like 60 positive, 40 negative? Like a little sports book kind of thing. And it's actually very helpful to make predictions and check them. It helps us know where we're actually at. And then we learn an extra thing about ourselves, which isn't just how we did, but we also learn how we thought we were going to do.

practiceDiscussion.speaker: Dale
practiceDiscussion.text: I was wondering if you could dedicate after something that you've been doing mentally gets easier, that it feels lighter, that you start to feel like, oh, maybe that's a blessing. I think that would be the perfect time to dedicate to the Buddhas.

practiceDiscussion.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceDiscussion.text: Yeah, any time. Any time we do any kind of virtue, we can definitely dedicate that, Dale. So it's great. Just catch as many of those opportunities as possible.

conclusion.speaker: Kadam Kyle
conclusion.text: Okay, I think that's it. We'll just dedicate now. We can think through the virtues you've collected through practicing, meditating, discussing. May all living beings find lasting peace of mind, enlightenment. We can dedicate to overcome our delusion of choice. Imagine what that would look like.
